author: danial-_-khan
quote:
I genuinely cannot believe Rockstar spent over a decade making this game just to deliver something so unnecessarily complicated, ridiculously overhyped and, quite frankly, disappointing.

After waiting 13 years, I expected a revolutionary gaming experience. Instead, I got a glorified relationship simulator with occasional gunfights and a map so unnecessarily detailed that you'd think Rockstar was trying to distract us from the actual gameplay.

Jason and Lucia are supposedly the heart of the story, but their entire relationship feels like watching two financially irresponsible criminals repeatedly make the worst possible decisions and somehow expect different results. The Bonnie and Clyde concept sounded fantastic on paper, but apparently the writers decided that emotional dependency and criminal incompetence were sufficient substitutes for an interesting storyline.

And don't even get me started on the pacing. The game somehow manages to make a criminal conspiracy spanning an entire state feel like an unnecessarily long administrative procedure.

The biggest plot twist is that Jason and Lucia actually have a baby named Tomás. Yes, that's right. Two people whose primary professional skill is committing increasingly stupid crimes are somehow responsible for an infant. Lucia literally leaves her baby at a diner during a robbery, gets arrested, and then spends the opening of the game begging police to let her go back. Absolutely phenomenal parenting. Truly the Bonnie and Clyde of questionable childcare decisions. Kotaku

The gameplay isn't much better. Apparently, Rockstar decided that robbing a convenience store should require the strategic planning of a military operation. You've got CCTV, safes, disguises, security systems, getaway planning and an entire financial management application called BuckMe. I'm playing Grand Theft Auto, not applying for a business loan.

The wanted system has six levels, which sounds impressive until you realise that escaping the police now requires more preparation than actually committing the crime. God forbid you forget to change your outfit after robbing someone.

And somehow, despite having an enormous map, the story manages to lose momentum in its later chapters. The game is so committed to making everything cinematic that sometimes I feel like I'm watching an expensive television series with occasional interactive advertisements.

Even the endings are apparently multiple-choice exercises in emotional disappointment. Instead of giving players one satisfying conclusion, Rockstar decided to make the outcome dependent on choices, because apparently 13 years wasn't enough time to write one definitive ending. Some endings are happier than others, but even that sounds like a low bar for a game about two criminals trying to build a future together. Kotaku

Final verdict:

GTA 6 is what happens when a company spends billions of dollars perfecting the water reflections, NPC schedules, gym animations and the way sweat appears on someone's back, only to forget that some people actually want to play a video game.

The graphics are fantastic. The world is detailed. The sound design is excellent.

Unfortunately, I bought Grand Theft Auto, not Grand Theft Relationship Counselling.

I'd give it a 0/10, but the loading screens deserve at least a 1.

Would I recommend it? Absolutely not. Wait another 13 years for GTA 7. Maybe by then Lucia will have learned not to leave her baby unattended during a robbery.
